rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer: You need 53 blocks, with 16 active threads in the final block and 176 extra threads outside the array. Assuming “bounce check” means “bounds check”: 10,000 = 52 × 192 + 16, so 52 full blocks plus one partial block cover every element. rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions serializable. Both transactions can read the same old snapshot, pass their checks, and update different rows, so no write–write conflict prevents either commit.

For example, two doctors are on call, and at least one must remain. Each transaction sees the other doctor on call and takes its own doctor off call; both commit, leaving nobody on call. Atomicity guarantees each transaction happens entirely or not at all—it does not protect a cross-row invariant from write skew. Serializable isolation, or appropriate locking that forces these checks to conflict, prevents this.
rows.usefulPrefix: Snapshot isolation makes each transaction atomic, but it does not make concurrent transactions serializable.
rows.note: Two concurrent snapshots eachseeotheron-call, disjointrowsupdatebothcommit violatescross-rowinvariant; atomicity≠serializability, serializableorconflictinglocking appropriate.

rows.name: candidate-failed-waveform
rows.question: Your bounds separated observations from assumptions. Switch to cooling: two kilograms of well-mixed water starts at sixty degrees Celsius in a room held at twenty degrees. It reaches forty degrees after ten minutes and thirty after twenty. Specific heat is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. Vessel heat capacity is negligible; no evaporation or internal heating occurs. Heat-loss power equals constant conductance times water temperature minus room temperature. Derive conductance with units. [Interviewer pause: one point five seconds.] A later run starts at sixty and reaches twenty-seven after twenty minutes; its constant ambient temperature was not logged. Construct two exact explanations, one retaining conductance and one retaining twenty-degree ambient. What experiment distinguishes them?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch to cooling two kilograms of well mixed water starts at sixty degrees Celsius in a room held at twenty degrees It reaches forty degrees after ten minutes and thirty after twenty specific heat is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per kelvin. Vessel heat capacity is negligible no evaporation or internal heating occurs Heat loss power equals constant conductance times water temperature minus room temperature Derive conductance with units interviewer pause one point five seconds a later run starts at sixty and reaches twenty seven after twenty minutes its constant ambient temperature was not logged Construct two exact explanations one retaining conductance and one retaining twenty degree ambient What experiment distinguishes them
rows.answer:
The original conductance is 14 ln(2) ≈ 9.70 watts per kelvin. The later endpoint can be explained exactly by either a colder room or greater conductance.

The water’s heat capacity is mc = 2 × 4,200 = 8,400 J/K. Writing conductance as G, energy balance gives
8,400 dT/dt = −G(T − A),
so T(t) = A + (60 − A) exp(−Gt/8,400), with time in seconds.

Originally A = 20°C. After 600 seconds, the excess temperature halves from 40 to 20 kelvin, so G = 8,400 ln(2)/600 = 14 ln(2) W/K. After 1,200 seconds it quarters, predicting 30°C, consistent with the second observation.

Explanation one: retain that conductance. At twenty minutes the exponential factor is 1/4, so 27 = A + (60 − A)/4. This gives a constant ambient temperature of exactly 16°C.

Explanation two: retain the 20°C ambient. Then 7/40 = exp(−1,200G/8,400), giving G = 7 ln(40/7) ≈ 12.20 W/K.

To distinguish them, repeat the later-run setup while independently logging room and water temperatures throughout cooling, ideally holding the room at a verified 20°C. With the original conductance, the twenty-minute temperature is 30°C; with the increased conductance, it is 27°C. The unlogged endpoint alone cannot distinguish ambient temperature from conductance.

rows.name: original-candidate-context-why
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer:
Because one endpoint cannot distinguish a colder room from stronger heat transfer: both make the water cool faster.

The energy balance is 8,400 dT/dt = −G(T − A), so T(t) = A + (60 − A)e^(−Gt/8,400). In the original run, the temperature excess halves every 600 seconds, giving G = (8,400/600)ln 2 = 14 ln 2 ≈ 9.70 W/K; the twenty-minute measurement confirms this.

For the later run, retaining that conductance gives a twenty-minute decay factor of 1/4, so 27 = A + (60 − A)/4, hence A = 16°C. Alternatively, retaining A = 20°C gives 7/40 = e^(−1,200G/8,400), hence G = 7 ln(40/7) ≈ 12.20 W/K.

Measure the room temperature during the later run to distinguish these explanations directly. Alternatively, measure the water after ten minutes: the two models predict 38°C and approximately 36.73°C, respectively.
